chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn al-Walid, from Yunus, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said: Ten men were sitting, and in their midst was a bag containing one thousand dirhams. Some of them asked others, 'Is this bag yours?' They all said, 'No.' Then one of them said, 'It is mine.' He was asked, 'To whom does it belong?' He replied, 'To the one who claims it.'

key_terms.أَلْفُ دِرْهَمٍ: One thousand dirhams, a unit of currency
key_terms.كِيسٌ: A bag or sack used for holding money or goods
key_terms.لِلَّذِي اِدَّعَاهُ: To the one who claimed it (the principle of ownership by assertion)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal principle regarding ownership when multiple people are present with an item and one claims it?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* within the chapter on proofs, this hadith illustrates the legal maxim *al-malu li man idda'ahu* (wealth belongs to the claimant) through a practical scenario of ten men and a bag of a thousand dirhams. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that in the absence of external evidence, the burden of proof lies on the claimant, yet the initial possession or assertion often determines immediate ownership until contested. This narrative serves as a foundational example for understanding how oral testimony and simple assertion function as valid *bayyinah* (proof) in civil disputes.
